question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,7)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & ={0}^{2}+{1}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\  & =0+1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-7 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,7)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=x+7\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+7$ (or $x-z+7=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.
